extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of fiction; students of narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and applying classical (Aristotelian) tale structure to a short narrative: the required parts (Protasis, Epitasis, Catastasis, Catastrophe/Peripeitia) and what each should accomplish. Grounded in the narrator's commentary in this 18th‑century fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to Aristotelian tale parts and order
rubrics_metrics.description: A tale should contain the essential integrant parts—Protasis, Epitasis, Catastasis, and Catastrophe/Peripeitia—and these parts should grow one out of the other in the order Aristotle established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slawkenbergius asserts that every tale in his decades is 'tied down' to this rule; without these parts, or without them appearing in their proper sequence, 'a tale had better never be told at all.' The parts must interlock so that the action develops causally and culminates in a proper peripeteia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protasis (first entrance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening section (Protasis) should introduce the personae dramatis and touch in the characters while slightly beginning the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: 'From his first parley with the centinel, to his leaving the city of Strasburg... is the Protasis' — i.e., initial encounters and setup that acquaint reader with characters and premise without yet heightening the central action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitasis (heightening / middle action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Epitasis should more fully enter upon the action and heighten it toward the central state or Catastasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It typically corresponds to the second and third acts; the narrator frames the busy period of the tale (e.g., the nights of uproar, lectures, disputes) as the Epitasis where incidents ramp up and stakes increase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catastasis (ripening toward climax)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Catastasis is the ripening phase in which incidents and passions mature in preparation for the final burst (peripeteia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the period after the Epitasis when events are 'ripening' for the fifth act; in the example it spans from the learned embarking on the dispute to their sailing away, setting up the conditions for the catastrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catastrophe / Peripeitia (resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Catastrophe or Peripeitia is the tale's conclusion: the unwinding of the labyrinth and the transformation from state of agitation to rest/quiet for the hero and the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator labels this the part he intends to relate and emphasizes that it should follow from the preceding parts. In practice it is the unravelling and restorative outcome that resolves the story's tensions.
